short: From 332 CE, Constantine bound tenant farmers, the coloni, to the land they worked, a step later law hardened into hereditary status.
full:
In 332, Constantine issued a constitution requiring agricultural tenants, coloni, to remain on the estates where they were registered, and empowering landowners to have runaway tenants returned in chains. The measure aimed to stabilise the tax base and the rural labour supply at a time when land was easier to find than the people to work it, particularly after the upheavals of the third century.

Later fourth- and fifth-century law extended the restriction to tenants' children, effectively making the tie to the land hereditary and blurring the legal line between a free tenant and a slave. The colonate outlived the western empire itself, forming one of the institutional roots of medieval serfdom across the territories Rome had once governed.
